title: The KYC Wall
summary: Brightbank is a digital-only banking app — customers open an account, verify their identity, and manage their money without ever visiting a branch. Its customers are everyday consumers acquired through paid ads, and the bank earns on deposits, card spend, and upgrades, but only once an account is verified and live.

Q1.text: KYC completion dropped to 60% this month; nearly all of the loss is at the document-upload step of identity verification. What do you do first?

choices.text: Compare drop-off across document types (passport, licence, ID card)
choices.reveal: Passport, licence and ID-card uploads complete at nearly identical rates — the type of document isn't the problem.

choices.text: Pull the timing: how long after upload do users abandon, and what are they shown during the wait?
choices.reveal: Most users who abandon do so 30–90 seconds after a successful upload, while the 'verifying…' screen is up.
choices.because: It looks at the delay between a successful upload and the result, which is where the loss actually happens before jumping to a fix.

choices.text: Interview users who abandoned during verification
choices.reveal: Interviews confirm the wait is the pain: 'I didn't know if it was working or if it ate my document.'

choices.text: Add a progress animation to the verifying screen right away
choices.reveal: The animation ships quickly, but abandonment barely moves — the fix assumed the problem was boredom, not uncertainty.

Q2.text: Document type isn't the problem: users complete upload at similar rates regardless of document. Where do you look next?

choices.text: Review the upload error states with engineering

reveal.text: Upload error rates are under 2% — errors are not driving a 40% loss.

choices.text: Segment abandonment by device and user age
choices.reveal: Abandonment is flat across segments — this is not a niche-device problem.

choices.text: Check what happens between upload and the verification result
choices.reveal: After upload, users see a bare 'verifying…' screen with no estimate, no reassurance, and no way to leave safely.
choices.because: It follows the evidence to the silent gap between upload and verification, rather than studying a problem that is not there.

Q3.text: Users abandon 30–90 seconds after a successful upload, during the verification wait. What's the strongest next step?

choices.text: Define the requirement: users must know the wait is normal, how long it takes, and that leaving is safe
choices.reveal: Defining the requirement sharpens the design work that follows — every option is now judged against those three needs.
choices.because: The wait data pins the loss to a 30-90 second uncertainty window, so the fix can address the right moment.

choices.text: Move KYC to a later point in the journey so fewer users hit it
choices.reveal: Deferring KYC is viable for some features, but regulation means core money movement can't start before verification — so for the core journey the wait experience is the work.

choices.text: Reduce verification time by switching providers
choices.reveal: Provider benchmarks show a possible 20-second improvement, but that is a procurement project measured in quarters, not this month.

Q4.text: The problem is framed: users don't know if the wait is normal or if leaving is safe. What do you design?

choices.text: A completion notification by email or push, so users can leave freely
choices.reveal: Notifications help, but tests show they don't calm the first 90 seconds — the on-screen story still needs to carry it.

choices.text: A status screen with a time estimate, what happens next, and explicit 'you can close this and return' copy
choices.reveal: The design pairs the estimate with a reassurance line; usability tests show users stop treating the wait as a failure state.
choices.because: It names the real failure - uncertainty during the wait - before shipping anything, which is what lets the fix land.

choices.text: A live-chat option in case verification fails
choices.reveal: Chat adds confidence for a few, but the dominant fear is 'is this stuck?', which chat doesn't answer.

Q5.text: The animation shipped and abandonment is unchanged. What now?

choices.text: Instrument the exact abandon moment and re-run the timing analysis
choices.reveal: Timing data shows abandonment clusters 30–90 seconds after upload — the animation never addressed the uncertainty.
choices.because: The timing evidence clears both fixes from the list, so the work goes to the wait experience itself.

choices.text: Keep the harmless animation and restart from evidence
choices.reveal: The animation stays, but the real work is the wait experience — back to the data.

choices.text: Accept the flat result and move on to the next roadmap item
choices.reveal: The metric stays at 60% — the KYC wall remains for every new user.

Q6.text: The new verifying screen passed usability tests — users understand the wait and that leaving is safe. Before rollout, what do you do?

choices.text: Roll it out to everyone and monitor support tickets
choices.reveal: Ticket volume about verification drops, but without a comparison group you can't attribute the change cleanly.

choices.text: A/B the new screen against the old on the next 10% of new users, watching KYC completion

reveal.text: Completion on the new screen climbs from 60% to 71% in the first week of the test.

table.caption: KYC screen completion, first week of the test

choices.because: An A/B test on the next 10% of users turns the completed-screen gain into proof instead of a good story.

choices.text: Document the 'honest wait' pattern for the design system
choices.reveal: The pattern is documented for reuse, but the KYC completion effect is still unverified.

criteria.label: Following the timing evidence
criteria.guidance: Abandon clusters at a delay, not a tap — measure where the loss happens before fixing anything.

criteria.label: Designing the wait experience
criteria.guidance: State the wait plainly: normal, how long, and safe to leave.

criteria.label: Proving the fix worked
criteria.guidance: A comparison group turns "it got better" into evidence.
